title: Column generation in one worked example

blocks.text: 11.3.4 Column Generation in One Worked Example

GridCap's vegetation program has its season's tasks counted: 48 spans to trim, 30 hazard trees to remove, 22 corridors to clear, 14 rights-of-way to widen and 17 sites of storm debris. Each kind of task takes a known number of minutes, and one crew-day has 600 minutes of work in it. The vegetation manager asks: how few crew-days cover the season? A crew-day is a **pattern**: so many tasks of each kind that fit in 600 minutes. There are hundreds of possible patterns, and on a real season with dozens of task kinds there are millions. **Column generation** solves the problem without listing them: it starts with a handful, and asks a small optimization problem, the **pricing problem**, for the one pattern that would improve the plan most, until no pattern would. This lesson walks one example end to end: the model, the first iteration by hand, the loop, the integer answer, and a check against a compact model solved directly.

The program is adapted from the OR-Tools MathOpt example `cutting_stock.py`, which cuts boards into pieces; here a crew-day is "cut" into tasks. The task data is invented for the lesson; GridCap is a fictional utility.
The Model

**Sets.** $`K`$ the kinds of task (trim span, hazard tree, clear corridor, widen right-of-way, storm debris); $`\Pi`$ every feasible pattern, a pattern $`p`$ being a vector of whole numbers $`a_{k,p}`$, the tasks of kind $`k`$ done in one crew-day with pattern $`p`$.

**Parameters.** $`w_k`$, the minutes one task of kind $`k`$ takes (55, 110, 250, 340, 190); $`d_k`$, the tasks of kind $`k`$ to do this season (48, 30, 22, 14, 17); $`W = 600`$, the minutes in a crew-day. A pattern is feasible when $`\sum_k w_k\, a_{k,p} \le W`$ and $`0 \le a_{k,p} \le d_k`$.
**Variables.** $`\lambda_p \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}`$ for every $`p \in \Pi`$: the number of crew-days worked with pattern $`p`$. In code, `days_0`, `days_1`, …
**Objective.**
\min \; \sum_{p \in \Pi} \lambda_p
**Constraints.**
\sum_{p \in \Pi} a_{k,p}\, \lambda_p \;\ge\; d_k \qquad \forall k \in K \qquad \text{(cover}_k)

Five rows and one column per pattern: a tall, thin matrix of the kind lesson 2.2.2's simplex never sees all of at once. The rows are $`\ge`$, not $`=`$: a crew-day may finish a task kind early and do fewer of something than its pattern allows (the OR-Tools sample writes equalities; with $`\ge`$ the duals below are never negative, which keeps the pricing problem simple).
Each Column Is a Pattern, and the Master LP Needs Only a Few of Them

Column generation works on the LP relaxation first ($`\lambda_p \ge 0`$, continuous) over a **restricted master**: the same rows with only some of the columns. It starts from the simplest patterns, one kind of task per day, as many as fit:

for t, (minutes, need) in tasks.items():          # start: one single-task day per task
    add_pattern({t: min(need, day // minutes)})
A column enters the MathOpt model with an objective coefficient of 1 and its counts in the cover rows, the way the OR-Tools sample adds one:

lam = master.add_variable(lb=0, name=f"days_{len(patterns)}")
master.objective.set_linear_coefficient(lam, 1)
for t, count in pattern.items():
    cover[t].set_coefficient(lam, count)
`first_pricing.py` builds that first restricted master and solves it with GLOP:

trim span            55 min x 48 tasks   start day: 10 per day
hazard tree         110 min x 30 tasks   start day:  5 per day
clear corridor      250 min x 22 tasks   start day:  2 per day
widen right-of-way  340 min x 14 tasks   start day:  1 per day
storm debris        190 min x 17 tasks   start day:  3 per day
master LP: 41.467 crew-days

With single-task days the LP needs 48/10 + 30/5 + 22/2 + 14/1 + 17/3 = 41.467 days. That is a feasible LP plan of the restricted master, so the full master LP's optimum is at most 41.467. The question is which pattern to add.
The Master's Duals Price Each Task, and the Pricing Problem Finds the Best New Day

Read the dual value $`\pi_k`$ of each cover row (lesson 2.3.3): the crew-days one more task of kind $`k`$ would cost the current plan. A new pattern $`p`$ costs one crew-day and does the work of $`\sum_k \pi_k a_{k,p}`$ crew-days at those prices, so its **reduced cost** (lesson 2.3.3) is
\bar c_p \;=\; 1 - \sum_{k \in K} \pi_k\, a_{k,p}.

A pattern with $`\bar c_p < 0`$ would lower the LP's optimum if added; if no pattern has one, the restricted master's optimum is the full master's (the simplex optimality test of lesson 2.2.2, applied to columns not yet written down). Finding the most negative reduced cost is itself an optimization problem over all patterns, the **pricing problem**, here a bounded integer knapsack:
v^* \;=\; \max \; \sum_{k \in K} \pi_k\, a_k \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{k \in K} w_k\, a_k \le W, \qquad a_k \in \{0, 1, \dots, d_k\} \;\; \forall k \in K \qquad \text{(day)}
`colgen.price_pattern` writes it in MathOpt and solves it with HiGHS (the OR-Tools sample uses CP-SAT):

m = mathopt.Model(name="pricing")
a = {t: m.add_integer_variable(lb=0, ub=need, name=f"a_{t}") for t, (_, need) in tasks.items()}
m.add_linear_constraint(sum(minutes * a[t] for t, (minutes, _) in tasks.items()) <= day, name="day")
m.maximize(sum(prices[t] * a[t] for t in tasks))
The first iteration, by hand and by program:

prices (crew-days per task): trim span 0.100, hazard tree 0.200, clear corridor 0.500, widen right-of-way 1.000, storm debris 0.333
pricing: best day {'clear corridor': 1, 'widen right-of-way': 1} worth 1.500 days of work, reduced cost -0.500

Each price is one over the tasks a single-task day holds: a widen-right-of-way task takes a whole day of its own (price 1.000), a corridor half a day. A day doing one corridor and one widening uses 250 + 340 = 590 minutes and does 1.5 days' worth of the current plan's work: reduced cost −0.5. Add it, and the LP improves.
<!-- practice 1 -->
Stop When No Day Has a Negative Reduced Cost; the Pricing Value Bounds the LP on the Way

Each iteration re-solves the master LP with the new column. `mathopt.IncrementalSolver`, as in the OR-Tools sample, keeps GLOP's model between solves and receives only the added column (lesson 4.3.4 covers incremental solving):
solver = mathopt.IncrementalSolver(master, mathopt.SolverType.GLOP)

The `lower` line is a bound that holds before the loop ends. Every pattern does at most $`v^*`$ at prices $`\pi`$, so the scaled prices $`\pi / v^*`$ are dual feasible for the *full* master LP; by weak duality its optimum is at least $`\sum_k (\pi_k / v^*) d_k`$, and $`\sum_k \pi_k d_k`$ is the restricted master's optimum $`z_{RMP}`$ (strong duality, lesson 2.3.2). So
\frac{z_{RMP}}{v^*} \;\le\; z_{LP} \;\le\; z_{RMP}.
The same argument, one step at a time:

items: **What dual feasible means here.** The full master LP's dual has one price $`\rho_k \ge 0`$ per task kind, and one row per pattern: $`\sum_k a_{k,p}\, \rho_k \le 1`$ for every $`p \in \Pi`$ (a pattern's work, valued at the prices, is worth at most the one crew-day it costs). Any such $`\rho`$ gives $`z_{LP} \ge \sum_k \rho_k d_k`$ (weak duality, lesson 2.3.2).

**The restricted master's prices may break some of those rows.** $`\pi`$ satisfies the rows of the patterns already in the master, but a missing pattern can be worth more than 1 at $`\pi`$. The pricing problem finds the worst one: no pattern is worth more than $`v^*`$.

**Dividing by $`v^*`$ repairs every row at once.** With $`\rho = \pi / v^*`$, each pattern's worth is divided by $`v^*`$ too: $`\sum_k a_{k,p}\, \pi_k / v^* \le v^* / v^* = 1`$. The prices stay nonnegative, so $`\rho`$ is dual feasible.
**Its value is the restricted master's optimum, scaled.** That is $`\sum_k \rho_k d_k = \bigl(\sum_k \pi_k d_k\bigr) / v^* = z_{RMP} / v^*`$, and step 1 makes that a lower bound on $`z_{LP}`$.

blocks.text: The code divides by $`\max(v^*, 1)`$: when no pattern is worth more than 1, $`\pi`$ is already dual feasible and needs no scaling, and the bound is $`z_{RMP}`$ itself.
The loop prints both sides, keeping the best lower value seen:

iter  1  master LP  41.467  best bound  27.644  best day worth 1.500  reduced cost -0.500  [1 clear corridor, 1 widen right-of-way]
iter  2  master LP  34.467  best bound  31.333  best day worth 1.100  reduced cost -0.100  [1 trim span, 2 clear corridor]
iter  3  master LP  34.067  best bound  31.938  best day worth 1.067  reduced cost -0.067  [2 hazard tree, 2 storm debris]
iter  4  master LP  33.500  best bound  31.938  best day worth 1.050  reduced cost -0.050  [3 hazard tree, 1 clear corridor]
iter  5  master LP  33.283  best bound  31.938  best day worth 1.050  reduced cost -0.050  [6 trim span, 1 clear corridor]
iter  6  master LP  33.100  best bound  33.100  best day worth 1.000  reduced cost +0.000  [5 hazard tree]
LP optimum 33.100 after 6 master solves, 10 columns; no plan uses fewer than 34 crew-days

The master LP falls from 41.467 to 33.1 and the bound rises from 27.644 to 33.1; at iteration 6 the best day is worth exactly 1, no day has a negative reduced cost, and the two meet. Five columns were added to the five starting ones: 10 columns out of the hundreds that exist. Because a crew-day count is a whole number, the LP optimum 33.1 proves that **no plan uses fewer than 34 crew-days**. A loop stopped early would still give an honest interval, for example $`[31.938, 33.5]`$ after iteration 4.
Integer Answers Come From the Generated Columns, and the LP Bound Says How Good They Are

The LP answer uses fractional days. The simplest way to an integer plan is **price-and-branch**: make the generated columns integer and solve the restricted master once as a MIP (the sample does the same):

integer master over those columns: 34 crew-days
   2 x  10 trim span  (550 min)
   2 x  5 hazard tree  (550 min)
   1 x  3 storm debris  (570 min)
  14 x  1 clear corridor, 1 widen right-of-way  (590 min)
   7 x  2 hazard tree, 2 storm debris  (600 min)
   2 x  3 hazard tree, 1 clear corridor  (580 min)
   6 x  6 trim span, 1 clear corridor  (580 min)

34 crew-days, and the LP said no plan uses fewer: this plan is optimal, proved by the bound, not by listing patterns. That proof is luck of the data, not a property of the method. The best integer plan may need a pattern the LP never priced, and then the integer master over the generated columns ends above $`\lceil z_{LP} \rceil`$ with no proof either way. Closing that gap exactly needs **branch-and-price**, which generates columns at every node of a branch-and-bound tree; MathOpt has no built-in support for it, and it is beyond this lesson. The honest report in that case is the interval $`[\lceil z_{LP} \rceil,\ z_{IP}]`$.
Some days in the plan do more than the season needs (the integer master may over-cover a $`\ge`$ row); a planner drops those tasks from the last days.
<!-- practice 2 -->
A Compact Model of the Same Question Checks the Answer and Shows Why Patterns Help

OR-Tools' bin packing page writes the same kind of question with a variable per item and bin and a yes/no per bin. `compact.py` does that here: a whole-number variable $`n_{k,j}`$ for the tasks of kind $`k`$ on day $`j`$, a yes/no $`u_j`$ per day, cover rows, a 600-minute row per day, and $`u_j \le u_{j-1}`$ so days are used in order. Any upper bound on the days will do for the number of days; it uses 36:

m.add_linear_constraint(sum(minutes * n[t, k] for t, (minutes, _) in TASKS.items()) <= DAY * use[k],
                        name=f"day_{k}")

compact LP bound       32.383  -> proves at least 33 days
column generation LP   33.100  -> proves at least 34 days
compact MILP optimum   34 days (OPTIMAL); column generation found 34

Both agree on 34. The bounds do not: the compact model's LP relaxation is 32.383, the total minutes divided by 600 (19,430 / 600), and proves only 33. Its LP may split a 340-minute widening across two days; the pattern LP cannot, because every column is a whole day that really fits. That is the general reason column generation is used: the pattern formulation has a **stronger LP relaxation**, the same strength gap lesson 6.4.3 measured between aggregated and cumulative rows, at the price of exponentially many columns that the pricing problem lets you never write down. On this small season the compact MILP still solves. On a season with dozens of task kinds and hundreds of days, its weaker bound and its interchangeable days (any reordering of the days is the same plan, the symmetry lesson 6.7.3 breaks with ordering rows) work against branch-and-bound, while the pattern model keeps one row per task kind; this lesson does not measure that larger case.
The Model
The restricted master and its pricing problem, whole, as column generation solves them.
**Sets.** $`K`$ the task kinds; $`\Pi' \subseteq \Pi`$ the patterns generated so far.
**Parameters.** $`w_k`$, $`d_k`$, $`W`$ as above; $`a_{k,p}`$ for $`p \in \Pi'`$; $`\pi_k`$, the cover rows' duals after the last master solve.

**Variables.** Master LP: $`\lambda_p \ge 0`$, continuous, for $`p \in \Pi'`$ (integer, $`\lambda_p \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}`$, in the final price-and-branch solve). Pricing: $`a_k \in \{0, 1, \dots, d_k\}`$ for every $`k \in K`$.
**Restricted master.**
z_{RMP} \;=\; \min \sum_{p \in \Pi'} \lambda_p \qquad \text{s.t.} \qquad \sum_{p \in \Pi'} a_{k,p}\, \lambda_p \ge d_k \quad \forall k \in K \qquad \text{(cover}_k)
**Pricing problem.**
v^* \;=\; \max \sum_{k \in K} \pi_k\, a_k \qquad \text{s.t.} \qquad \sum_{k \in K} w_k\, a_k \le W \qquad \text{(day)}
**Loop.** Add the pricing answer as a new column while $`v^* > 1`$ (its reduced cost $`1 - v^*`$ is negative); then $`z_{RMP} = z_{LP}`$. At every iteration $`z_{RMP} / v^* \le z_{LP} \le z_{RMP}`$.
Summary

items: **Each column is a pattern, and the master LP needs only a few of them.** Start from simple patterns; the restricted master's optimum is an upper bound on the full LP.

**The master's duals price each task, and the pricing problem finds the best new day.** The reduced cost of a pattern is $`1 - \sum_k \pi_k a_{k,p}`$; the pricing knapsack finds the most negative one.
**Stop when no day has a negative reduced cost; the pricing value bounds the LP on the way.** $`z_{RMP}/v^*`$ is a lower bound at every iteration; here 6 master solves and 10 columns.
**Integer answers come from the generated columns, and the LP bound says how good they are.** 34 crew-days, proved optimal here by $`\lceil 33.1 \rceil = 34`$.
**A compact model of the same question checks the answer and shows why patterns help.** The compact LP proves only 33.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: one feasible way to fill a crew-day; one variable of the master
the master LP over the columns generated so far
finds the column with the most negative reduced cost (here a bounded knapsack)
$`z_{RMP} / v^* \le z_{LP}`$, valid at every iteration
solve the integer master over the generated columns once; a heuristic with a bound
columns generated at every node of a branch-and-bound tree; exact
re-solve the master after each added column
the new column's entry in a cover row
turn the columns integer for the final solve

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [OR-Tools MathOpt sample `cutting_stock.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/samples/python/cutting_stock.py) (the example adapted here: a leader LP over configurations solved with GLOP through `IncrementalSolver`, a knapsack worker on the leader's duals, a stop when the best configuration is worth at most 1 within a tolerance, and a final integer solve over the configurations generated); [Bin Packing (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/pack/bin_packing) (the compact formulation with a variable per item and bin and a yes/no per bin, the model `compact.py` writes); [Applied Mathematical Programming, Chapter 12, Large-Scale Systems (MIT 15.053)](https://web.mit.edu/15.053/www/AMP-Chapter-12.pdf) (section 12.8, column generation and the cutting-stock problem: columns too many to write down, produced by a subproblem on the current prices); [MathOpt (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/math_opt) (the modeling API used for the master and the pricing problem).
Challenges

items: Add a sixth task kind, "inspect span", 35 minutes, 60 tasks. Predict whether the LP optimum rises by more or less than $`60 \times 35 / 600 = 3.5`$ crew-days.
The pricing problem is a knapsack with five kinds. Solve it by dynamic programming over minutes instead of HiGHS, and check that the loop prints the same lines.
Write the cover rows as equalities, as the OR-Tools sample does. Which prices can now be negative, and what does a negative price mean for a task?
A second crew type works 480-minute days at the same cost. What changes in the master and in the pricing problem?

blocks.text: Design Note: The Pricing Problem Is the Only Place the Day's Rules Live

The master knows nothing about minutes: it only counts tasks covered and days used. Every rule about what one day can hold (the 600 minutes here, travel time between sites, a crew that cannot do widening work) belongs in the pricing problem. That separation is what makes column generation extendable: a new rule about a day changes one small model, and the master, its duals and its bound stay as they are.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**first_pricing.py.** The first restricted master, its prices and the first pricing answer (*the first two sections*). *Try:* Change the clear-corridor time from 250 to 260 minutes. Predict the best first day.

**colgen.py.** The loop with its bounds, and the integer master over the generated columns (*the third and fourth sections*); adapted from the OR-Tools sample `cutting_stock.py`. *Try:* Start with no single-task days but one day of each task. Predict whether the loop needs more master solves.
**compact.py.** The compact model, its LP bound and its MILP optimum (*A Compact Model of the Same Question*). *Try:* Remove the `order_` rows. Predict whether the MILP optimum changes.
